analysis.one_liner: Lets bankruptcy judges cut mortgage balances on foreclosed homes and rewrite loan terms.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 17-15 in December 2007, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1978, bankruptcy law has forbidden judges from changing the terms of a mortgage on a family's primary home — even while they can rewrite loans on vacation homes, cars, and investment property. This bill repealed that exception. A homeowner in Chapter 13 bankruptcy facing foreclosure could have had the loan balance cut to what the house was actually worth and paid off over a longer schedule. It also stopped lenders from quietly piling fees onto a mortgage during a bankruptcy case and waived the pre-filing credit counseling class for people whose lender had already started foreclosing.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure who owed more on their mortgage than the house was worth. A bankruptcy judge could reduce the secured debt to the home's current value, stretch payments past the usual five-year limit, and the family would keep the home. Homeowners in active foreclosure would also skip the mandatory (and paid) credit counseling session before filing.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 1978-era carve-out that shields primary-residence mortgages from modification in Chapter 13 bankruptcy, letting a plan alter the loan's terms [S2][S3].
Allows payment of the home-mortgage claim over a period longer than the normal Chapter 13 limit, easing monthly costs for a distressed borrower [S2][S3].
Bars a lender from adding fees, costs, or charges to the mortgage while the bankruptcy case is pending unless it gives timely notice to both the debtor and the trustee [S2][S3].
Waives the pre-petition credit counseling requirement for a Chapter 13 filer who certifies that foreclosure on their home has already begun [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors in mortgage-backed bonds. When a judge cuts a loan balance to the home's value, the difference between the old loan and the reduced claim is debt the lender never collects. Servicers also lose the ability to add fees during a case without notice.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argued that allowing judges to write down mortgages would raise the cost of mortgage credit for all future homebuyers, since lenders would price in the risk that a bankruptcy court could cut their collateral's loan balance.

The relief is not free housing: the bill keeps the lender's lien on the home until the modified claim is paid in full and carves the home mortgage out of the final bankruptcy discharge, so the family still owes the reduced amount [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a family on the edge of foreclosure, cutting the loan balance to the home's real value was the difference between keeping and losing the house — and unlike later bailout money, no public funds were involved; the loss fell on the lender who made the loan. The lender-side cost was real, and the standard objection about slightly costlier mortgage credit for everyone deserves weight, but in 2007's housing downturn the scale of the harm being prevented was far larger than the credit-cost objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared a subcommittee by one vote and won approval in the full Judiciary Committee 17-15, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Miller of North Carolina introduced the bill on September 20, 2007, with Reps. Linda Sanchez, Barney Frank, Carolyn Maloney, and Mel Watt as original cosponsors; it was sent to the Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S5].
It drew 88 cosponsors, 85 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S4].
The Commercial and Administrative Law subcommittee advanced it to the full committee by a narrow 5-4 vote on October 4, 2007 [S5].
On December 12, 2007, the full Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported with amendments by a 17-15 vote [S5].
After that committee vote the bill saw no further action — no report to the House floor, no vote — and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with the bill dead [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and the investors holding home mortgages came out ahead: because the bill died, no bankruptcy judge could cut their loan balances to the home's value or restrain fee additions during a case, and homeowners facing foreclosure lost a route to keep their homes. The timing mattered — the bill died just as home prices were collapsing nationwide.

for.name: Rep. Brad Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed allowing bankruptcy judges to modify primary-residence mortgages.

for.role: Committee members voting to report the bill
for.what_they_did: Voted 17-15 to order the amended bill reported out of committee.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote after the committee approved it.

against.name: 15 Judiciary Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting against reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted no in the 17-15 committee markup that ordered the bill reported.

against.name: Mortgage lenders and banking industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed allowing bankruptcy judges to reduce mortgage balances, arguing it would raise borrowing costs and destabilize mortgage finance.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 85 of the 88 cosponsors — and the committee votes were close (5-4 in subcommittee, 17-15 in full committee), though the record does not break those roll calls down by party.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and mortgage-backed securities investors
industries.note: The bill let a bankruptcy judge cut the secured claim to the home's current value, meaning the lender eats the difference between the loan and the house price. Blocking the bill preserved their legal right to collect the full mortgage balance even from a family losing the home.
They could no longer add fees, costs, and charges to a delinquent mortgage during a bankruptcy case without timely notice to the debtor and trustee, closing a channel of fee income.
The 2005 bankruptcy law made paid pre-filing counseling mandatory; the bill waived it for homeowners whose lender had started foreclosure, removing those filers as customers.
